name: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
title: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
answer: Lighting rigs and relighting cover the setup and control of light in a photograph or a rendered image, and the later adjustment of that light after the fact. In AI image work the term spans two related jobs: describing a lighting setup in a prompt so a model reproduces it, and taking an existing image and changing its illumination without reshooting. It sits between studio craft and image generation, and it is one of the main levers for making synthetic images read as photographic rather than flat.

sections.body: Lighting rigs and relighting cover the setup and control of light in a photograph or a rendered image, and the later adjustment of that light after the fact. In AI image work the term spans two related jobs: describing a lighting setup in a prompt so a model reproduces it, and taking an existing image and changing its illumination without reshooting. It sits between studio craft and image generation, and it is one of the main levers for making synthetic images read as photographic rather than flat.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on image generation and editing models, which this site tracks at around 1,000 live image generation models, alongside conventional editing software and, in some pipelines, 3D or rendering tools that supply a physically plausible light setup. Relighting specifically leans on models that accept a depth map, a normal map or a reference light direction, so the system needs some estimate of the scene's geometry, not just its pixels. Practitioners typically work on a desktop with a GPU, or through a hosted service, and keep the original capture or render as the reference point.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts by reading the light in the source image: direction, hardness, colour temperature, and how many sources are implied by the shadows and highlights. From there the practitioner either writes that description into a prompt, or feeds the image into a relighting model with a target direction or reference frame. Results are judged on whether shadows, specular highlights and contact shadows stay consistent with one another, since mismatched cues are what make a relit image look wrong. Iteration is normal, and the accepted output is usually composited back over the original rather than used whole.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions here are mostly about the source image, not the light: a relit portrait is still a derivative of the photograph it came from, so the licence on that photograph governs what can be done with it. Where a model was trained on photographs, the output can carry the same unresolved questions that sit behind the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits this site tracks. Provenance matters for the same reason, and practitioners generally keep the original file, the prompt or light parameters, and a record of which model produced the change. Likeness and publicity rights apply when the subject is a real person, and disclosure norms vary by publisher and client.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Relighting is moving toward models that infer scene geometry well enough to place a new light without a depth pass, which would remove most of the manual setup. The practical near term is likely tighter integration between generation and editing tools, so a light change is one step in a normal retouching workflow rather than a separate pipeline. The open questions are consistency across a set of images and honest provenance, since a convincing relight is hard to detect and easy to misrepresent.
